sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Error handling is one of the most opinionated aspects of Go and one of the most common interview discussion topics. Go deliberately chose errors-as-values over exceptions to make error paths explicit and to avoid the hidden control flow of try/catch. Every production Go codebase has patterns around wrapping, sentinel errors, and custom types, and interviewers test whether you know how to use them correctly and why the language made these choices.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: The error type is just an interface with one method: Error() string. Any type that implements it is an error. Errors form a chain through wrapping: fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err) stores the original error inside the new one. errors.Is walks that chain looking for a target by value; errors.As walks it looking for a target by type. Sentinel errors are package-level variables (var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")) used for identity comparison. panic is not an error — it is for truly unrecoverable situations, and recover should be used only at process boundaries (e.g., HTTP handlers).

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
• error is an interface: nil error means success; non-nil means failure.
• fmt.Errorf with %w: wraps the original error, preserving the chain for errors.Is / errors.As.
• errors.Is: checks identity (value equality) anywhere in the chain — use for sentinel errors.
• errors.As: unwraps to a concrete type anywhere in the chain — use when you need fields from a custom error.
• Sentinel errors: io.EOF, sql.ErrNoRows; define your own with errors.New at package level.
• Custom error types: structs implementing error, adding fields like StatusCode, Op, Path.
• panic/recover: panic unwinds the stack; recover catches it only inside a deferred function. Reserve for programmer errors and process boundaries.
• Error design: add context when propagating ("query users: %w"), but avoid over-wrapping.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
• 'What is the difference between errors.Is and errors.As?' — Is checks value identity; As checks type and unwraps to it.
• 'How do you add context to an error without losing the original?' — fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err).
• 'What is a sentinel error and when would you not use one?' — package-level variable; avoid when callers need structured data from the error.
• 'When is panic appropriate in Go?' — unrecoverable programmer errors (index out of range, nil dereference), or as a control mechanism recaptured at a top-level recover in HTTP middleware.
• 'How would you design errors for an API package?' — exported sentinel errors for known conditions + unexported custom type for structured detail.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "Go treats errors as ordinary values, which I appreciate because every error path is visible in the call chain — there's no silent exception escaping up the stack. My standard practice is to wrap errors with fmt.Errorf and %w as they propagate so callers can unwrap the chain with errors.Is or errors.As. For expected conditions — like a record not found — I define a sentinel error at the package level so callers can switch on it without string matching. For richer errors that carry extra context, like an HTTP status code or a database constraint name, I implement a custom struct type. I avoid panic except at true program boundaries like an HTTP handler's recover middleware, where I want to absorb any unexpected panic and return a 500 rather than crashing the whole server."
